To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a high degree of disagreement is not necessarily harmful in the long term; (2) stubbornness and withdrawal are harmful in the long-term; (3) the husband's behavior in the interaction is more predictive of change in marital satisfaction than the wife's behavior.

(a) the pattern of marital interaction that predicts concurrent marital happiness is different from the pattern that predicts change in marital happiness over time; and (b) the pattern that predicts improvement in marital happiness over 3 years is the same as the pattern that predicts deterioration in marital happiness over the same time period, and this pattern includes defensiveness, stubbornness, and withdrawal.

(a) marital interaction is a better predictor of concurrent marital satisfaction than of change in marital satisfaction; (b) some patterns of interaction that are harmful to marital satisfaction in the short run are beneficial in the long run; and (c) defensiveness, stubborness, and withdrawing from interaction are harmful to marital interaction in the long run.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying interaction patterns that may be dysfunctional in the maintenance of marital happiness and satisfaction.
the question of whether marital interaction is a cause or a consequence of marital satisfaction, and the results of our research suggest that it is both.
the development of a theory about the interactional processes of marriage and the ways in which these processes are related to the maintenance and deterioration of marital satisfaction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the marital interaction patterns that are most detrimental to marital satisfaction are defensiveness, stubbornness, and withdrawal from discussion.
the marital satisfaction of both spouses is best maintained by a pattern of interaction in which both spouses are actively involved in resolving problems.

marital interaction patterns are important for marital satisfaction in the long run, but that the patterns that are harmful in the short run are not always those that are harmful in long-run perspective.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

marital interaction patterns are more predictive of concurrent satisfaction than they are of change in satisfaction, and that some patterns that have been considered dysfunctional are in fact predictive of improvement in satisfaction.
the maintenance of marital quality over time is not simply a matter of the absence of negative interaction, but also a matter of the presence of positive interaction.
the maintenance of marital happiness depends on the ability of couples to engage in a high level of positive interaction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should not make assumptions about which patterns are healthy and which are harmful.
it may be important to distinguish concurrent and change effects of interaction patterns.
we need to look more at the long term consequences of marital interaction patterns.
